Date: 2026-08-27

Duration: 62 minutes

summary: Redwood Optimize walkthrough focusing on batching and TTL/cache tradeoffs for Nocturne's conversational summarization product. Covered prefix/KV cache strategies, TTL tuning vs lookup cost, sessionization patterns, and a high-level cost model. Agreed next steps: share cost simulator, run throughput sims, and provide sample prompts/heatmap.
transcript:
[00:00] Jordan Patel: Alright, good afternoon everyone, thanks for joining. We're on for about an hour; the plan is a quick context check then dive into Optimize recommendations for batching and your cache TTLs, and then a short cost sim. Maya will drive the demo.
[00:22] Ethan Rivera: Great, yeah, thanks. Quick note — our main product is a near real-time convo summarizer for customer support, typical sessions are 8-12 turns, sometimes long tails, and peak qpss are around 1k across ten endpoints. Latency SLO is 300 ms p95.
[00:45] Maya Chen: Good, that helps. When you say 300ms p95, is that end-to-end or just token generation?
[00:52] Priya Singh: End-to-end, from API call to returning final text. We accept streaming on some endpoints but many clients use a single batch call.
[01:10] Jordan Patel: Cool. Two quick qualifiers: do you run sticky sessions / session affinity today? And what's your current model and hosting — in-house hosted on k8s?
[01:22] Marcus Holt: We have affinity at the load balancer level right now, but it's coarse. We run our own GPUs on-prem, different clusters in three regions. We are looking at a hybrid move — some hosted inference maybe for dev and spikes.
[01:38] Maya Chen: That informs prefetch/prefix cache choices. For sessionized workloads with affinity you get higher hit rates on a per-worker KV, but if affinity is coarse you may get more misses and higher lookup cost.
[01:52] Ethan Rivera: We also worry about data retention; some of our sessions contain PII so we have to manage KMS and audit logs. SOC 2 is a must.
[02:04] Jordan Patel: Noted — Redwood Private and Dedicated both support customer-managed KMS and audit logs, we can include SOC 2 artifacts. We'll drop the security pack in the follow-up.
[02:15] Maya Chen: Okay jumping into the Optimize console — I'm going to share my screen. (brief shuffling) Apologies if the video quality is meh, network is iffy.
[02:34] [Screen share: Redwood Optimize console — model profile, batching controls, cache configuration]
[02:40] Maya Chen: First slide: high-level concept. We balance batching to hit GPU throughput while keeping latency within your 300 ms SLO. Second lever is cache strategy — prefix caching vs full-session KV. Prefix caching stores recent prefixes (n tokens) across sessions; session KV stores per-session key-value kv cache for continuing contexts.
[03:05] Priya Singh: Which one gives more wins for a summarization product?
[03:11] Maya Chen: Usually prefix caching reduces token compute for repeated prompts or system messages, so if you have repeated instruction templates or often start with the same context, prefix helps. Session KV is better when users resume long conversations because it avoids recomputing the entire context every time. But session KV increases memory since each session holds KV state.
[03:35] Jordan Patel: And the cost tradeoff — prefix cache has lookup cost per request; session KV has memory cost and can increase instance sizing. Maya, can you show the cost sim widget?
[03:47] Maya Chen: Yup. (navigates) Here you can set avg tokens per request, freq of repeated prefixes, TTL on kv lookups, batch size distribution, and we show estimated token-hour and GPU utilization.
[04:05] Ethan Rivera: In our telemetry, about 40% of calls contain the same 2-3 system prompts at the start — standardized instructions. The rest are user messages.
[04:18] Maya Chen: That suggests prefix cache will yield good wins. If you tune prefix TTL to be short — like 30s to 2 minutes — you capture bursts without holding KV forever. But note lookup cost: each cache check adds ~0.8-1.5ms in our hosted runtime depending on region. If your p95 budget is tight, we model total added latency.
[04:44] Marcus Holt: Do you handle cache-locality? If we use dedicated nodes, will the session KV remain on the same GPU?
[04:53] Maya Chen: On Dedicated yes — session affinity plus local KV reduces cross-node lookups. In hosted mode we use smart routing: we route to a node pool with the KV or fall back to recompute. There's a balance: routing to preserve KV may add a small routing latency but saves compute.
[05:12] Priya Singh: Show us an example number — like with our 1k peak, what percent cost reduction could we expect with prefix + short TTL?
[05:22] Maya Chen: On the sim I plugged in your numbers: 1k qps peak, avg 45 tokens generated, 40% prefix reuse. With a 60s prefix TTL, batching window 15-30ms and average batch size ~6, we estimate token compute reduction of ~28% and GPU-hour reduction roughly 22%, which translates to approximate monthly savings of 18-24% depending on committed pricing and instance types. These are sim estimates.
[05:55] Ethan Rivera: That's meaningful. What's the downside? Complexity of managing TTLs, eviction flaps?
[06:03] Maya Chen: Two main risks: stale cache leading to quality drift if you cache prompt templates that change; and memory pressure on session KV if you set TTLs too long. Also, aggressive batching can add tail latency if bursts are very spiky.
[06:18] Jordan Patel: On quality drift — Redwood Optimize supports per-prompt eval hooks; you can instrument a small eval set and alert if outputs change post-caching. We can automate regressions tied to prompt sets.
[06:31] Marcus Holt: About TTL — do you recommend uniform TTL or adaptive TTL based on session heat?
[06:38] Maya Chen: Adaptive TTL often gives best of both worlds. We can set a baseline TTL and then extend for hot sessions detected by our heatmap: hot sessions get longer TTLs or sticky placement; cold sessions expire faster. That reduces global memory while preserving hit rates for high-frequency sessions.
[06:58] Priya Singh: How does this interact with your prefix lookahead / prefetch capability?
[07:05] Maya Chen: Good question. Prefetching proactively loads likely next prefixes into cache at the end of a response. If your UI tends to send follow-up messages quickly, prefetch can raise hit rates. The trade is extra lookups and occasional wasted prefetches. Combine prefetch with short TTLs and prefetch cancellation heuristics to reduce waste.
[07:28] Ethan Rivera: We get many aborted sessions — users open the chat and immediately close. That would waste prefetch if aggressive.
[07:34] Maya Chen: Right — our sim includes an abandonment parameter. For your profile, we modeled 25% abandonment and tuned prefetch aggressiveness down; net still positive because of the high prefix reuse on successful sessions.
[07:49] [10-minute mark omitted for brevity — discussion of infra mapping and security brief]
[08:12] Jordan Patel: Quick security note — for PII, you'd want either Dedicated or Private. Both support customer-managed KMS. We can provide SOC 2 artifact bundle and HSM options for key wrapping.
[08:25] Ethan Rivera: OK we will need the SOC 2 pack.
[08:29] Jordan Patel: We'll attach it to the follow-up email.
[08:33] Maya Chen: Back to cost model — one nuance is batching window vs tail latency. If you set batching too aggressively to increase batch size, low-latency requests may see extra queuing. For your 300ms SLO, we recommend a max batching delay of 20-30ms and dynamic cutoffs that drop requests into a lower-latency lane at high percentiles.
[08:56] Priya Singh: Is dynamic lane routing part of Optimize or a config in Redwood runtime?
[09:02] Maya Chen: It's runtime-level with Optimize suggestions. The console will propose thresholds based on your heatmap and p95 targets and will surface expected hit rates and GPU utilization per lane.
[09:17] Marcus Holt: Any gotchas with model quantization? We currently run fp16 but considering int8 to save memory on session KV.
[09:26] Maya Chen: int8 can reduce memory and throughput cost, but watch for quality regression on summarization tasks. Optimize includes sample-eval A/B tests to flag regressions. For KV cache size, quantization usually helps but you need to test end-to-end.
[09:40] Ethan Rivera: Let's talk about concrete config for us — what's a starting point?
[09:45] Maya Chen: Start with prefix caching enabled for common system prompts, TTL=60s, batching delay=20ms with adaptive batching that reduces delay under spike, prefetch disabled initially. Session KV enabled only for long-running endpoints where continuity matters, TTL=300s with eviction LRU and memory cap per node. Run 1 week of sims.
[10:06] Jordan Patel: I'll put those in a template and share the cost-sim inputs.
[10:10] Priya Singh: Can you also simulate worst-case cold start cost if affinity is lost? We have incidents where affinity flickers during scale events.
[10:19] Maya Chen: Absolutely — we model affinity loss by adding a cold-start penalty that forces full recompute for a percent of requests; I ran a 10% affinity-loss scenario and the savings go down from 22% to about 12% — still positive but you lose half the benefit. So improving affinity/sticky placement is high leverage.
[10:42] Ethan Rivera: Any immediate operational knobs we could try without infrastructure changes?
[10:47] Maya Chen: Yes — enable prefix caching for the system prompts only (low-risk), set TTL=30-60s, add batching window at 20ms, and monitor p95. No infra changes required. If you like the results, we can propose Dedicated routing with session locality.
[11:03] Jordan Patel: Let's talk timeline — if we get sample prompts and heatmap by Monday, Maya can run sims mid-week and we can reconvene to review results. If sims look good, we scope a POC for Dedicated pilot.
[11:16] Ethan Rivera: Sounds good.
[11:18] [wrap-up, short crosstalk]
[11:25] Jordan Patel: Quick recap: 1) Jordan sends cost-simulator + template config, 2) Nocturne sends prompts + heatmap, 3) Maya runs sims and shares results, 4) decide on POC. Also Jordan will attach SOC 2 docs and KMS notes.
[11:40] Priya Singh: One last question — any limitations on number of KV entries per node? We have huge number of concurrent short sessions historically.
[11:48] Maya Chen: We set memory caps per node; Optimize suggests per-node caps and an LRU with TTL fallback. For extreme short-session traffic, prefix caching tends to be lighter weight because it stores canonical prefixes not session blobs. We can share a sizing guide.
[12:06] Ethan Rivera: Thanks everyone. We'll get the artifacts over.
[12:10] Jordan Patel: Thanks all, expect the follow-up email with sims template and security pack.
[12:17] [call ends]

Notes: transcript contains occasional mis-transcribes (e.g., "qpss" instead of "qps", "K V cache" sometimes written as "K-V cache"). Shared artifacts: link to cost-simulator spreadsheet (https://redwood.example.com/sims/nocturne-cost-sim), SOC2 pack link placeholder (docs attached in follow-up).
